t: Maximum Value after Insertion — Placing One Digit Greedily
o: We hold the decimal string of a possibly negative integer n — digits 1-9 only, up to 10^5 characters — and one digit x (1-9) that may be inserted at any position except left of the minus sign, aiming to maximize the resulting number. Positive case: inserting 6 into 73 between 7 and 3 gives 763, beating 673 and 736. Negative case: inserting 2 into -55 before the first 5 gives -255, which beats -525 and -552 because its magnitude is smaller. Example 1 shows ties change nothing: any slot for 9 inside 99 yields 999. Example 2 enumerates the candidates -213, -123, -132 for n = -13 with x = 2, confirming -123 wins. Because the string can be 10^5 characters long, repeatedly materializing or comparing whole candidates is off the table; the placement decision must come from one scan.
k: All candidates share one length, so among positive numbers lexicographic digit order equals numeric order — and it reverses for negatives.
Positive n: insert x before the first digit strictly smaller than x; append if none exists.
Negative n: maximize value by minimizing magnitude — insert x before the first digit strictly greater than x; append if none.

a.i: Construct all len(body)+1 candidates by inserting x at each position of the unsigned body, then keep the extreme under the correct comparator: greatest body when n is positive, least when negative. Equal lengths make plain string comparison valid. Simple and obviously correct, but each of O(L) comparisons may inspect O(L) characters — quadratic worst case, too slow at L = 10^5.
s: Strip any leading minus sign, remembering it.
Build every candidate by inserting str(x) at positions 0 through len(body).
Track the lexicographically greatest candidate for positive n, the least for negative.
a.t: O(L^2) — up to L candidates, each comparison scanning up to L characters in the worst case.

a.i: The comparator logic collapses into one left-to-right scan. For positive n walk past digits >= x and stop at the first digit < x: inserting there pushes the bigger digit as far left as possible. For negative n walk past digits <= x and stop at the first digit > x, so x slides under a larger digit and adds as little magnitude as possible. Falling off the end appends x, which ties provably favor anyway.
s: If n starts with '-', start at index 1 and advance while digit <= x; otherwise advance from index 0 while digit >= x.
Insert x exactly at the stopping index (the loop naturally appends when no digit qualifies).
a.t: O(L) — one pass to find the slot; building the output is unavoidable.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary beyond the output string.

w: State the equal-length/lexicographic observation first in an interview — it is what licenses the greedy scan. Pitfalls: flipping comparisons for negative numbers, using non-strict inequalities on the wrong side (equal digits should be passed; placing later is never worse), and forgetting x can equal existing digits. Follow-ups: minimize the value instead (swap comparators), or insert an entire substring rather than one digit.
